We took one prisoner aboard" (first day of the carrier strikes on Tokyo). Others: Irons's essay on the Haynsworth Association website (haynsworth-org:20230208204038/dd700-photos/prisoners/prisoners.html) has the boat seen by a lookout 7000 yards off the port bow and destroyed by "Forty rounds" of 5-inch, and puts the whole day "On the morning of February 16th"; the diary's rounds are kept. Morison (vol. 14, p. 24) and Herder (Naval Siege of Japan, p. 26) give only the afternoon action, as three boats.

"At 1352 smoke was observed on the horizon ... identified as two Jap pickets which had been strafed by our planes. We opened fire with our 5" batteries, and sunk both pickets after expending 86 rounds of 5"/38 AAC. One prisoner from the first, and ten prisoners from the second picket were taken aboard. Three of these suvivors were seriously wounded. These were transferred along with two others to C.T.F. 58 in BUNKER HILL, at 1700" (12 prisoners in the day). Others agree on 12: the battle-star citation quoted by Irons (Irons, Phalanx, 228: "three Japanese picket boats ... twelve Japanese POW while about 70 miles SE of Tokyo"; the diary's 0800 and 1200 fixes are 115-125 nm from Tokyo, bearing about 140) and Irons's essay on the Association website (haynsworth-org:20230208204038/dd700-photos/prisoners/prisoners.html: "Eleven more", two fighters leading the ship to the smoke, three wounded and two others to Bunker Hill). Herder (Naval Siege of Japan, p. 26, caption to NARA 80-G-308465) has nine survivors.
"At 1640, the entire Task Force commenced retiring to the South" (afternoon strikes on Tokyo cancelled for weather)
